did_you_know.text: The tribe of Simeon received land inside Judah’s territory — in biblical allocations tribal borders could overlap.
Beersheba was an important desert oasis and crossroads — a major water source and regional center in the Negev.
Ziklag appears in the Samuel narratives as the town where David stayed while fleeing Saul.
'Chatzar' in allotment lists often means the town together with its outlying farmyards and villages — the urban center plus its rural space.
Place names beginning with 'Ain' point to a spring or water source — such water sites were natural settlement centers.
Zebulun is linked to the sea in Jacob’s blessing, yet its allotment here includes inland valleys like Jezreel — poetic images and actual borders can differ.
Zebulun’s towns lie by the Jezreel Valley — one of the most fertile farming areas in ancient Israel.
Shunem also appears in the prophetic stories — the Shunammite woman’s story with Elisha is told in Kings.
Borders reaching the Jordan gave tribes access to key valleys and routes — the Jordan corridor was a major travel and trade axis.
Asher’s land reached the northern coast near Phoenician cities like Tyre and Sidon — bordering areas with different cultural influences.
The name 'Carmel' is related to 'kerem' (vineyard) — Mount Carmel was known in antiquity for its fertility.
Asher is listed with twenty-two towns — indicating dense settlement along the coast and nearby plains.
Naphtali’s allotment lay in the north, including highlands and pasturelands extending toward Mount Hermon.
The 'Kinneret' mentioned here is the same Sea of Galilee known today as the Kinneret.
The Danites captured Laish/Leshem in the north and renamed it Dan — a well-known case of a tribe relocating under external pressure.
At Tel Dan archaeologists found an ancient inscription that mentions the 'House of David' — an important find for the study of biblical history.
Shiloh was Israel’s early cultic center before Jerusalem — casting lots in the land division was seen as leaving the decision to God.
